In casual talk, calling someone a devil can be a playful insult, especially for a child or a rascal. In polite company, the word is used less in strong religious speech and more in fixed expressions.

distinctions.note: Satan is the proper name used in Scripture for the adversary of God, while devil is the common noun for the same figure or for an evil spirit generally.
A demon is an evil spirit in general, while devil usually refers to the chief evil spirit in Christian belief.

collocations: the devil made me do it

examples.everyday: Oh, you little devil, you finished the cookies before dinner!
examples.professional: The devil is in the details, so let's check every line of the contract before we sign.
examples.analytical: In Mark's Gospel, the devil appears as a real opponent, and that portrayal shapes how the early church understood temptation.

nuance.analogy: The devil in Christian belief is like a shadow that opposes light: real in its effect, but defined by what it turns away from.
nuance.etymology: From Old English deofol, from Late Latin diabolus, from Greek diabolos, 'slanderer, accuser'.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the second syllable as 'vuhl' with a strong vowel, rather than a quick reduced sound.
Using 'devil' in formal writing as a casual insult, which can sound jarring.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, the devil is the adversary of God and of humanity. The Hebrew word is satan, meaning 'adversary' or 'accuser,' and the Greek word is diabolos, meaning 'slanderer' or 'accuser.' Matthew 4:1 says Jesus was led into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. Revelation 12:9 identifies the great dragon as the ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan. 1 Peter 5:8 warns believers that their adversary the devil prowls around seeking someone to devour.

devil.etymology: From Middle English *devil*, *devel*, *deovel*, from Old English *dēofol*, from **diubul*, from Latin *diabolus*, ultimately from Ancient Greek *διάβολος* (“false accuser, slanderer”), also as "Satan", from *διαβάλλω* (“to slander”), literally “to throw…

senses.definition: To join or participate in (a conference call).
senses.example: Did you dial in to that earnings announcement?

senses.definition: To configure or set up (particularly a complex machine with many configuration options.
senses.example: Before starting the recording, make sure you've dialed in the right synthesizer settings.

senses.definition: To connect (to a system or service) by telephone.
senses.example: I tried dialing in to the server, but I couldn't connect.

senses.definition: To apprehend and align oneself (to an idea, circumstance, way of thinking, etc.).
senses.example: The company quickly dialed in to the fact that customers wanted greater convenience.

senses.definition: To reduce (something) to an appropriate level.
senses.example: He was pushy, but he dialed that in until they found him tolerable.

senses.definition: To achieve a perfect result in brewing coffee by manipulating grind size, water amount, etc.

core.definition: To join a phone or video meeting by calling in, or to adjust something carefully until it works well.

pronunciation.tip: The particle IN is stressed, because in phrasal verbs the second word usually carries the main stress. The word dial is reduced to dy-uhl, and the two words link so that it sounds like dy-uh-LIN.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it is friendly and practical, and in the sense of fine-tuning it suggests skill and care.
nuance.usage_note: In American workplaces people say dial in to mean join a conference call, and it is very common in meeting invitations. Dial into is also used. In the fine-tuning sense, you might say let's dial it in, meaning let's get the details exactly right. A natural reply is I'll dial in now or sounds good.

distinctions.note: Log in means to access a computer system or account, while dial in means to join a call or adjust something precisely.
Call in can mean to phone a radio show or work, while dial in specifically refers to joining a conference or system by phone.
Tune is a general word for adjusting something; dial in suggests more precise, careful fine-tuning, often with settings or numbers.

examples.everyday: I can't make it to the family dinner, but I'll dial in on speakerphone so I can hear everyone.
examples.professional: Please dial in five minutes early so we can test the audio before the client joins.
examples.analytical: To dial in a model is to adjust its hyperparameters until its performance meets the target, a process that can look like tuning but depends on careful, repeated measurement.

nuance.analogy: To dial in is like tuning a radio until the station is clear, turning the knob slowly until the sound is just right.
nuance.etymology: From dial, to call by telephone or adjust, plus the particle in.
common_mistakes: Saying dial the meeting, which is not natural; use dial into or dial in to the meeting.
Pronouncing it with equal stress on both words; the particle IN carries the stress.

dial-in.etymology: *dial* + *in*, from tuning in to a radio frequency by changing the dial, or dialling a telephone number.

conversation.text: I'll dial in from the car.
Can you send me the dial-in number?
It took a while to dial in the settings on the new camera.
If the video doesn't work, you can dial in by phone.
Three people dialed in late, so we started over.

senses.definition: To separate into two parts, to classify into two classes, or to categorize into two categories.
To be divided into two.
To exhibit as a half disk.

core.definition: To divide something into two distinct, usually opposite, parts or categories, often by a clear cutoff point.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the 'KAH' syllable, and the final syllable rhymes with 'size'. Keep the middle vowel reduced and do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a process of division, though it can imply oversimplification in an argument.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dichotomize mainly in statistics, research methods, and academic writing, as in 'dichotomize the outcome into yes or no'. In everyday speech they would say 'split into two groups' or 'divide into two categories'. Using it in casual talk can sound overly technical.

distinctions.note: Categorize means to sort into any number of groups, while dichotomize specifically means dividing into exactly two.
Split is a common everyday word, while dichotomize is precise, technical, and suggests a sharp binary division.

examples.everyday: The survey asks people to just pick yes or no, which kind of dichotomizes their answers.
examples.professional: For the classifier, we dichotomize the churn label into churned and retained customers.
examples.analytical: When we dichotomize a continuous variable, we discard information and may distort the true relationship.

nuance.analogy: To dichotomize is like cutting a pizza exactly in half and calling the two halves the only slices that matter.
nuance.etymology: From dichotomy plus -ize, from Greek dichotomia 'a cutting in two'.
common_mistakes: Using dichotomize for dividing into three or more parts.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying dy-KOT-uh-mize.

senses.definition: The state of being disinclined; want of propensity, desire, or affection; slight aversion or dislike.
senses.example: strong disinclination

core.definition: A feeling of not wanting to do something; a mild reluctance or lack of desire.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on -NAY-, and the -tion ending is pronounced shun. Watch the -ng- in the middle, which is a single nasal sound before k, not 'ing-glee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a mild or polite unwillingness, usually without strong negative feeling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use disinclination in everyday talk; they say 'I don't really feel like it' or 'I'm not into it.' It appears in formal writing, polite refusals, and reports, such as 'He showed a disinclination to commit to the timeline.' For casual use, 'reluctance' or 'hesitation' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Reluctance is more common and more active, suggesting resistance; disinclination is a milder lack of desire.
Aversion is a strong dislike; disinclination is a much weaker feeling.

examples.everyday: I have a disinclination to drive in snow, so I usually take the train.
examples.professional: The manager showed a clear disinclination to approve new hires until the budget was reviewed.
examples.analytical: Her argument rests on a historical disinclination among scholars to accept oral sources as evidence.

nuance.analogy: Disinclination is like a door that is not locked but is also not swinging open; you could go through, but you are not drawn to.
nuance.etymology: From dis- (not) and inclination (tendency or leaning).
common_mistakes: Using 'disinclination' in very casual speech, where it sounds stiff.
Using 'disinclination' when you mean a strong dislike; use 'aversion' for that.

senses.definition: The act of displacing, or the state of being displaced.
The act of dislocating, or putting out of joint; also, the condition of being thus displaced.
A linear defect in a crystal lattice. Because dislocations can shift within the crystal lattice, they tend to weaken the material, compared to a perfect crystal.
A sentence structure in which a constituent that could otherwise be either an argument or an adjunct of a clause occurs outside of and adjacent to the clause boundaries.
In men's gymnastics, a rotating of the shoulders when performing a backwards turn on the still rings. Many skills in acrobatics appear to involve dislocating a joint, when they actually do not.
The displacement of parts of rocks or portions of strata from the situation which they originally occupied.

core.definition: The state of a bone being moved out of its joint, or the state of something being moved out of its normal place or order.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KAY, the syllable before -shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in medical and technical use; negative when describing social or personal disruption.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say dislocation most often in medical settings or when describing economic or social disruption, such as job dislocation after factory closures. In casual speech people say the bone popped out or the joint is out. In economics and policy writing, dislocation for displaced workers is a standard phrase.

distinctions.note: Displacement is the more general term for being moved from a place; dislocation often implies disruption or damage to a joint, a system, or a community.
A sprain stretches ligaments without moving the bone; a dislocation moves the bone out of its joint.

examples.everyday: The doctor said the shoulder dislocation was clean, so they just popped it back in place.
examples.professional: Automation caused real job dislocation in the plant, so we are funding retraining for the affected workers.
examples.analytical: The essay traces the cultural dislocation that followed migration, in which people lost the familiar structures that had given their lives order.

nuance.analogy: A dislocation is like a train that jumps the track: the parts are still there, but they are no longer aligned or working together.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin dislocatio, from dislocare, 'to put out of place'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of KAY.
Using dislocation in everyday talk for a simple injury where sprain is more natural.

dislocation.etymology: From Middle English, from Old French, a borrowing from Medieval Latin *dislocātiō*, *delocatio*.

senses.definition: The act of displacing, or the state of being displaced; a putting out of place.

The weight of a ship or other floating vessel, traditionally measured or calculated by finding the volume of the vessel below the waterline when afloat, the weight of the displaced liquid being equal to that of the whole displacing body.
Moving the target to avoid an attack; dodging.
The capability of a communication system to refer to things that are not present (that existed or will exist at another time, or that exist at another location).
The transfer of feelings or emotions from their intended recipient to another object or person.
The amount of liquid displaced by a submerged object.
The transfer of electricity along tubes of induction and thereby polarizing a dielectric.
Ellipsis of engine displacement.
A vector quantity which denotes distance with a directional component.
(dated) The process of extracting soluble substances from organic material and the like, whereby a quantity of saturated solvent is displaced, or removed, for another quantity of the solvent.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: The act of moving something out of its place, or the number of people forced from their homes, or the weight of water a ship pushes aside.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PLAYS, and the ending -ment is a reduced schwa plus m and t. Do not add an extra vowel between the m and the t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use displacement in news about people forced from homes by war, climate events, or development, and in engineering and physics for water displacement or a ship's weight. In everyday talk they say 'moved out' or 'forced to leave'. In psychology, it can mean redirecting feelings toward a safer target, though that sense is less common.

distinctions.note: Relocation is usually a planned move chosen by a person or company; displacement implies being forced out or moved out of place involuntarily.
Migration describes movement of people or animals over distance, often voluntary or seasonal; displacement suggests disruption or compulsion.

examples.everyday: The flood caused a lot of displacement in our town, so my neighbors are staying with relatives.
examples.professional: Our report tracks the displacement of households after the storm so the housing team can prioritize assistance.
examples.analytical: Arendt's analysis of statelessness shows that displacement is not only a physical movement but a loss of the political standing that makes a person's claims recognizable.

nuance.analogy: Like water rising in a bathtub when you climb in, displacement is what happens when something takes up the space that was there before.
nuance.etymology: From displace, with the suffix -ment, from Latin dis- and locus 'place'.
common_mistakes: Using displacement for 'replacement' in ordinary speech; say replacement for swapping parts.
Confusing the physics sense with the people sense, which can cause confusion in mixed discussions.

senses.definition: To disguise or conceal something.
To feign, dissimulate.
To deliberately ignore something; to pretend not to notice.
To falsely hide one's opinions or feelings.

core.definition: To hide your true feelings, intentions or knowledge by pretending, often by acting as if you do not know or care about something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on SEM, the second syllable. The b is usually silent in the ending -mbəl, so it sounds like dih-SEM-buhl.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies dishonest concealment, though it is less harsh than outright lying.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dissemble mostly in writing, news analysis, or formal speech about politicians, witnesses or public figures who avoid direct answers. In everyday talk, you would more likely say 'dodge the question' or 'act like you don't know'. It is a good word for a serious critique, but it sounds stiff in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Lie means to say something false; dissemble means to hide the truth through pretense or evasion, which can be done without saying anything false.
Evade means to avoid something, such as a question; dissemble adds the idea of pretending or disguising your real feelings.

examples.everyday: My brother tried to dissemble when Mom asked about the broken window, but his face gave him away.
examples.professional: The vendor seemed to dissemble about the delay, so we asked for the timeline in writing.
examples.analytical: Scholars argue that the author must dissemble his true views to avoid censorship.

nuance.analogy: Like wearing a mask at a party: you may look relaxed, but your real face is hidden.
nuance.etymology: Alteration of dissimble, from Latin dissimulare, 'to dissemble'.
common_mistakes: Confusing dissemble with disassemble, which means to take apart.
Pronouncing the ending as -bul with a clear b; the b is nearly silent.

dissemble.etymology: First attested in the beginning of the 15th century, in Middle English; Middle English *dissemblen*, borrowed from Old French *dissembler*, itself borrowed from Latin *dissimulō* and modified after *sembler*, *semblance*, etc.

senses.definition: In a distinctive manner; in a way that is notable for its difference.
senses.example: The British Shorthair has a distinctively chunky body, dense coat and broad face.

core.definition: In a way that is clearly different from others and easy to notice or recognize.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on 'STINGK', and the final syllables are reduced: 'tiv' is short and 'lee' is a clear 'ee' sound. Avoid adding extra syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it describes a clear, noticeable quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'distinctively' in writing and formal speech to describe style, voice or design, such as 'distinctively American'. In casual talk people more often say 'really different' or 'you can tell right away'. It sounds polished and is not rude.

distinctions.note: 'Distinctly' means clearly or plainly, often about hearing or seeing. 'Distinctively' means in a way that makes something stand out from others.
'Uniquely' means in a one-of-a-kind way. 'Distinctively' means in a way that is recognizably different, though not necessarily unique.

examples.everyday: That bakery's bread tastes distinctively sweet, so I always know when I've bought it.
examples.professional: The new interface is designed distinctively, so users can tell our tools apart from competitors'.
examples.analytical: The novel is written distinctively, blending historical documents with the narrator's private voice.

nuance.analogy: Like a voice in a choir that you can pick out clearly even when everyone is singing.
nuance.etymology: From distinctive, from Latin distinctus, 'separated'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'distinctively' with 'distinctly' when you mean 'in a way that stands out'.
Pronouncing the middle vowel as a full 'ih' instead of a short, reduced sound.

senses.definition: To govern, rule or control by superior authority or power.
To exert an overwhelming guiding influence over something or someone.
To enjoy a commanding position in some field.
To overlook from a height.
To precede another node of a directed graph in all paths from the start of the graph to the other node.
Dominant.

(historical) The late period of the Roman Empire, following the principate, during which the emperor's rule became more explicitly autocratic and remaining vestiges of the Roman Republic were removed from the formal workings of government; the reign of any particular emperor during this period.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: To control or rule over something or someone, or to have the strongest influence in a situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle vowel to a quick 'uh'. The final syllable rhymes with 'gate'; don't add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it suggests strong control, sometimes unfairly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dominate in sports talk ('they dominated the game'), business news and everyday descriptions of a person who takes over a conversation. Saying someone dominates the conversation is a mild criticism, so use it carefully about people.

distinctions.note: Control can be simple and neutral; dominate suggests overwhelming power that overshadows others.
Lead means to guide or be ahead; dominate implies a more total, forceful advantage.

examples.everyday: My little brother always tries to dominate the conversation at dinner.
examples.professional: Two vendors dominate the cloud analytics market, so we need a backup plan.
examples.analytical: The author argues that economic metaphors have come to dominate public discourse about education.

nuance.analogy: To dominate is like a large wave that pushes every other swimmer out of the way.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dominari, 'to be lord, rule over'.
common_mistakes: Using dominate with a preposition, as in 'dominate over'; the verb takes a direct object.
Confusing dominate with dominant as a verb form.

dominate.etymology: Latin *dominātus*, perfect active participle of *dominor* (“to rule, have dominion”) (see *-ate*), from *dominus* (“lord, master”) + *-ō*.

senses.definition: A scalar λ, such that there exists a non-zero vector x (a corresponding eigenvector) for which the image of x under a given linear transformation A is equal to the image of x under multiplication by λ; i.e. Ax=λx.

core.definition: A scalar by which a linear transformation stretches or shrinks a special nonzero vector, without changing its direction.

pronunciation.tip: Stress EYE first, with the second part, 'val', stressed secondarily. Say 'val-yoo' with a clear 'yoo', and keep the hard 'g' in eigen.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eigenvalue constantly in math, physics, engineering, and data science. In meetings a data scientist might say 'the top eigenvalue' or 'the eigenvalues are close.' Non-experts rarely use it, so keep it for technical contexts.

distinctions.note: The eigenvalue is the scalar that scales; the eigenvector is the vector that keeps its direction.
A singular value is defined for any matrix and is nonnegative; an eigenvalue belongs to a square matrix and may be complex or negative.

examples.everyday: My friend in engineering said the eigenvalues told him the bridge model was unstable.
examples.professional: We sort the eigenvalues in descending order and keep the top five components for the dashboard.
examples.analytical: A matrix is diagonalizable if its eigenvalues yield a full set of linearly independent eigenvectors.

nuance.analogy: An eigenvalue is like the amount a rubber band is stretched along one special direction, while that direction itself stays the same.
nuance.etymology: From German eigen, 'own, characteristic', and value, from Latin valere, 'to be worth'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'EYE-gen-val-yoo' with the wrong vowel in the first syllable.
Using eigenvalue for any value of a matrix; it applies only to the scaling factor for an eigenvector.

senses.definition: A vector that is only scaled (not rotated out of its span) under a particular linear transformation; a left or right eigenvector depending on context; given a linear transformation A, a vector x such that Ax=λx [or xA=λx] for some scalar λ (called the eigenvalue).
A right eigenvector; given a matrix A, the eigenvector of the transformation "left-side multiplication by A."

core.definition: A nonzero vector that a linear transformation only stretches or shrinks, so it keeps its direction, scaled by its eigenvalue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress EYE first and VEK second, with a secondary stress on the -ur ending. The final syllable is the American r-colored 'er' sound, like 'tur'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; purely technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eigenvector in math, physics, machine learning, and data science. In a meeting a team member might say 'the first eigenvector points along the main trend.' Pronounce the final syllable with a clear American r sound.

distinctions.note: An eigenvector is a direction vector; an eigenvalue is the scalar that it is scaled by.
A vector is any element of a vector space; an eigenvector is a special vector that a given transformation only scales.

examples.everyday: My study partner says the eigenvector is the direction that stays put when you stretch the space.
examples.professional: We take the top eigenvector of the covariance matrix as the main direction of variation in the customer data.
examples.analytical: If Ax equals lambda x, then x is an eigenvector of A, and any nonzero multiple of x is also one.

nuance.analogy: An eigenvector is like an arrow on a rubber sheet that gets longer or shorter when the sheet is stretched, but never turns.
nuance.etymology: From German eigen, 'own', and vector, from Latin vector, 'carrier'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'eye-gen-VEK-tor' with a British-style final vowel.
Thinking the eigenvector changes direction; under the transformation it keeps its line.

senses.definition: A piano (from the number of keys)
A butterfly of the genera Callicore, Perisama, or Diaethria, some of which have a pattern on their wings similar to the digits "88".

core.definition: Informal name for a piano, from the 88 keys on a standard full-size instrument.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, EIGHT, more strongly than the first. Say 'ay-tee' quickly and keep the final 't' of eight, even though it is a flap in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; informal and somewhat playful, mainly used by musicians.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'the eighty-eight' informally to mean a piano, especially in jazz or pop circles. It is a casual nickname, not a formal name. In a music store or with a teacher, you would just say 'piano.' You may hear 'eighty-eights' as a plural for piano keys.

distinctions.note: Piano is the standard word; eighty-eight is an informal nickname based on the keys.
A keyboard can be a synthesizer or an electronic instrument with fewer keys; eighty-eight specifically implies a full piano range.

examples.everyday: Mom still plays the eighty-eight in the living room every Sunday.
examples.professional: The studio rents a full eighty-eight for recording sessions, so keep the tuner ready.
examples.analytical: The eighty-eight keys define the instrument's range, a fact that shapes how composers write for the piano.

nuance.analogy: Calling a piano the eighty-eight is like calling a car the four-wheeler: a nickname that points to one of its key features.
nuance.etymology: Formed from the English numerals eighty-eight, referring to the number of keys on a standard piano.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first word, as in 'AY-tee-ayt', which sounds wrong.
Using it in formal writing; use piano instead, or the 88-key piano when precision matters.

core.definition: A Hebrew name meaning 'oak' or 'terebinth'; it belongs to a Hittite man, to an Israelite judge, and to a town in Zebulun.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EE. The second syllable is 'lahn' with an open 'ah' sound, as in 'father'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a proper name with no special connotation outside Scripture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this name mainly in Bible study or when discussing biblical history. Do not confuse it with the common English name 'Elon,' which is pronounced the same way and is widely used as a surname.

distinctions.note: Two or three different people or places share this name; the context of each passage shows which is meant.

examples.everyday: I'd never heard of the judge Elon before, but the Bible study leader said he ruled Israel for ten years.
examples.professional: In the reading plan, the session on the minor judges includes Elon, whose ten-year rule is recorded in a single verse.
examples.analytical: The brief notice of Elon the Zebulunite, who judged Israel and was buried in the land of Zebulun, shows how the book of Judges passes over some leaders in few words.

nuance.analogy: Like a family name shared by many people in one community, Elon appears for several people in Scripture, so the surrounding verses tell you which one is meant.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew 'elon', 'oak' or 'terebinth', a type of tree.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (eh-LON); the stress falls on the first syllable.
Mixing up the judge Elon with other judges like Ehud or Shamgar.
nuance.biblical_note: Elon is a Hebrew name meaning 'oak' or 'terebinth.' Several people and one place bear the name in Scripture. In Genesis 26:34 Elon the Hittite is the father of Esau's wife Basemath. In Judges 12:11-12 Elon the Zebulunite judges Israel for ten years and is buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun. In 1 Kings 4:9 Elon-beth-hanan is named as a town in the district of Solomon's officials.

elon.etymology: From a trade name, presumably a shortened form of the chemical name.

senses.definition: The state of being elusive.

core.definition: The quality of being hard to catch, pin down, or understand.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LOO, as in the adjective. Be careful with the ending: 'siv-nus' has a short, unstressed final syllable, not 'nes'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a quality, often used when describing something frustrating or mysterious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use elusiveness more in writing and formal discussion than in casual speech. In conversation, people usually say 'it's hard to pin down' or use the adjective elusive. The noun works well in reviews, reports, and essays about something that resists explanation.

distinctions.note: Evasiveness is deliberate avoidance of questions or responsibility; elusiveness is the quality of being hard to catch or define, with no intent implied.

examples.everyday: I love the elusiveness of good coffee shops here; you have to find them by accident.
examples.professional: The elusiveness of the bug is why the release was delayed twice.
examples.analytical: The elusiveness of moral certainty is central to the book's argument about conscience.

nuance.analogy: Elusiveness is like a shadow that moves as you approach it.
nuance.etymology: From elusive plus the suffix -ness, which forms a noun of quality.
common_mistakes: Using elusiveness when you mean evasiveness, which implies deliberate avoidance.
Stressing the wrong syllable; say 'ih-LOO-siv-nus', not 'EE-loo-siv-ness'.

senses.definition: To retain (someone) as an employee.
senses.example: Our company employs hundreds of people.

senses.definition: To provide (someone) with a new job; to hire.
senses.example: Yesterday our local garage employed a new mechanic.

senses.definition: To use (someone or something) for a job or task.
senses.example: The burglar employed a jemmy to get in.

senses.definition: To make busy; to preoccupy.
The state of being an employee; employment.
senses.example: The school district has six thousand teachers in its employ.

core.definition: To hire someone to work for pay, or to use something for a particular purpose.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, PLOY, with the diphthong 'oy' as in 'boy'. Do not stress the first syllable or change the vowel to 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In a workplace it simply means hiring, and in other uses it means using something skillfully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use employ most often in business, news and formal writing, as in 'the company employs 300 people'. In everyday talk people more often say 'hire' or 'work for' when talking about jobs, and 'use' for tools or methods. 'Employ' sounds more official than 'hire'.

distinctions.note: Hire is the everyday word for bringing someone on as a worker, while employ is more formal and can also mean keeping someone on a payroll.
Use is the general word for applying something, while employ suggests using something skillfully or for a specific purpose.

examples.everyday: The diner down the street employs three cooks and two servers, and they're always looking for more help.
examples.professional: We plan to employ two more data engineers next quarter to keep up with the new reporting work.
examples.analytical: Weber's analysis shows how modern bureaucracies employ formal rules to justify their authority.

nuance.analogy: To employ someone is like plugging a tool into a project: you choose it, bring it in and put it to work.
nuance.etymology: From Old French employer, from Latin implicare 'to enfold, involve'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'employ to' a company, when the usual phrase is 'be employed by' or 'work for'.
Using 'employ' for everyday hiring talk such as 'I want to employ a plumber' when 'hire' sounds more natural.

employ.etymology: From late Middle English *emploien*, *imploien*, *emplien* (“to apply to a specific purpose”), from Anglo-Norman *emploier*, Old French *emploiier* (“to entangle, fabricate, to make use of”), ultimately from Latin *implicō* (“to infold, entangle, involve,…

senses.definition: To wear away by abrasion, corrosion, or chemical reaction.
senses.example: The cliff is gradually being eroded by the waves.

senses.definition: To destroy gradually by an ongoing process.
senses.example: to erode a person’s trust

core.definition: To gradually wear away something, or to weaken and destroy it little by little over time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, ROHD. The first syllable is a reduced 'ih', and the r is a strong American r. Do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes slow damage, loss, or decline.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'erode' for physical wear, like cliffs or soil, and for things that weaken over time, like trust or public support. It is common in news, business, and everyday speech. In casual talk, people often say 'wear down' or 'break down' for the same idea.

distinctions.note: 'Wear down' is the more casual, everyday phrase, while 'erode' sounds more formal or precise.
'Corrode' specifically means damage by chemical reaction, especially to metal, while 'erode' covers gradual wearing away by any force.

examples.everyday: Constant small lies can slowly erode the trust between friends.
examples.professional: The repeated outages are starting to erode the team's confidence in the release process.
examples.analytical: Market competition can erode the moral sensitivity that institutions once relied upon for their legitimacy.

nuance.analogy: Erode is like water on a stone: no single drop breaks it, but enough drops change its shape.
nuance.etymology: From Latin erodere, 'to gnaw away', from e-, 'out', and rodere, 'to gnaw'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'erode' with 'erupt' or 'erase', which have different meanings.
Using 'erode' for sudden destruction; it means gradual wearing away.

senses.definition: US standard spelling of aetiology.

core.definition: The study of the causes of a disease or condition, or the cause or origin of something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on AH, the third syllable, and the first two syllables are both clear 'ee' sounds. Americans most often spell it 'etiology', and the ending 'jee' is soft.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise medical or scientific term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans spell this word 'etiology', the US form of the older British 'aetiology'. It is used mainly in medicine, epidemiology, and academic writing. In everyday speech people say 'cause' or 'origin'.

distinctions.note: Cause is general and everyday, while etiology is a technical term about the study or theory of causes, especially for diseases.
Pathology is the study of disease processes and structure, while etiology focuses on why the disease starts.

examples.everyday: The doctor said they still don't know the etiology of my headaches, so she ordered more tests.
examples.professional: The incident review focused on the etiology of the outage, not on who was on call.
examples.analytical: A theory of sin's etiology must explain how a universal human inclination arises without making God the author of evil.

nuance.analogy: Etiology is like tracing a river back to its spring: you look for where the flow began.
nuance.etymology: From Greek aitia (cause) and -logy (study of).
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling 'aetiology' in American writing.
Confusing etiology with ecology, which is the study of organisms and their environments.

senses.definition: To kill, especially as punishment for a capital crime.
senses.example: There are certain states where it is lawful to execute prisoners convicted of certain crimes.

senses.definition: To carry out; to put into effect.
senses.example: Your orders have been executed, sir!

senses.definition: To perform.
senses.example: to execute a difficult piece of music brilliantly

senses.definition: To start, launch, or run.
senses.example: to execute a program

senses.definition: To run, usually successfully.
senses.example: The program executed, but data problems were discovered.

senses.definition: To carry out, to perform an act; to put into effect or cause to become legally binding or valid (as a contract) by so doing.
senses.example: to execute a contract

core.definition: To carry out a plan, order, task or command, or to put a rule or decision into effect.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is weak. The final syllable is a long 'oot' sound with a y glide: 'kyoot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the business and technical sense. In the sense of killing as punishment it is strongly negative and serious.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English execute mostly appears in professional or technical settings, such as executing a plan, a trade or a program. Americans prefer carry out or do for casual speech. The sense of putting someone to death is legal and news-oriented.

distinctions.note: Carry out is more natural and flexible in everyday speech, while execute is more formal and precise.
Perform emphasizes doing an action or show, while execute emphasizes completing a plan or command reliably.

examples.everyday: I'll execute my plan for the weekend and let you know how it goes.
examples.professional: We executed the migration overnight, and the rollback script is ready if anything fails.
examples.analytical: The theory fails if the institution cannot execute its own principles in practice.

nuance.analogy: Like a chef turning a written recipe into a finished dish.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exsequi, to follow out or carry out to the end.
common_mistakes: Using it casually for everyday tasks like cooking dinner; use carry out or make instead.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: The English word execute usually translates Hebrew asah (to do, make) and related terms for carrying out justice or judgment. Jeremiah 33:15 speaks of the Lord's promise to execute justice and righteousness in the land. Psalm 149:7 describes the execution of vengeance on the nations. Both passages stress carrying out a just decision rather than a bare act of killing.

execute.etymology: From Old French *executer* (French *exécuter*), from Latin *exsecutus*, past participle of *exsequor* (“to follow”), from *ex-* (“out”) + *sequor* (“to follow”).

senses.definition: Explanation or interpretation of a text, especially a religious text; also, the academic study of this; an instance of this.
Critical commentary or discussion; an instance of this.
(historical) In full numeral exegesis: a procedure formerly used to solve algebraic equations.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Careful explanation or interpretation of a text, especially Scripture, drawing out its original meaning through study of language, context, and history.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable: JEE. The first syllable has secondary stress, and the middle 'uh' is reduced. Don't say 'ek-ZEE-jee-sis' or pronounce the g as hard.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it implies disciplined, careful reading.
nuance.usage_note: Used mainly by seminary faculty, pastors, and scholars. In casual talk, Americans would say 'interpretation' or 'what the passage means.' The plural is 'exegeses' (ek-suh-JEE-seez).

distinctions.note: Eisegesis reads one's own ideas into a text, while exegesis draws the meaning out of it.
Hermeneutics is the theory of principles of interpretation; exegesis is the actual practice of interpreting a passage.
A commentary is a written work containing exegesis; exegesis is the interpretive process itself.

examples.everyday: Our pastor spent twenty minutes on one verse, and honestly, I loved the exegesis.
examples.professional: The seminary course combines Greek exegesis with practical preaching skills.
examples.analytical: Her exegesis of Romans 5 shows that the argument depends on the Adam-Christ parallel rather than on isolated proof texts.

nuance.analogy: Exegesis is like carefully unpacking a suitcase to see what is inside, rather than stuffing in your own belongings.
nuance.etymology: From Greek exēgēsis, 'a leading out, explanation,' from ex- 'out' + hēgeisthai 'to lead.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable: say ek-suh-JEE-sis.
Confusing it with eisegesis, which is the opposite practice.
Using it for any casual opinion rather than for a text-based interpretation.
nuance.biblical_note: The word is not a biblical term, but the Greek verb exēgeomai appears in John 1:18, where the Son 'has made him known,' literally explained the Father. Luke 24:27 describes Jesus interpreting to the disciples the Scriptures concerning himself, a model of exegesis. Nehemiah 8:8 describes the Levites giving the sense of the Law so the people understood the reading.

exegesis.etymology: Late Latin *exēgēsĭs* (“exposition”), or from its Ancient Greek *ἐξήγησῐς* (“explanation, interpretation; narration”), from *ἐξηγέομαι* (“to guide, lead; to expound, interpret; to explain, relate”) + *-σῐς*.

senses.definition: The quality of being meagre or scanty.

core.definition: The condition of being small, scanty or meager in amount, size or resources.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the -gyoo- syllable, with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. The final -ity is 'uh-tee', not 'ih-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It describes a sense of smallness or lack, often in a formal or critical tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exiguity rarely and mostly in formal or literary writing, such as essays, reviews or academic prose describing scarce resources or small spaces. In everyday talk people say 'scarcity', 'small size' or 'tiny amount'. Use it sparingly, since it may sound pretentious in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Scarcity focuses on a lack of something needed, while exiguity describes the small or meager quantity or size itself.
Paucity is more common in academic writing and means a small or insufficient amount; exiguity emphasizes smallness and meagerness more.

examples.everyday: The apartment's exiguity made it hard for us to fit a couch and a table at the same time.
examples.professional: The exiguity of our test data limited how confidently we could generalize the model's results.
examples.analytical: The exiguity of the surviving sources makes any firm claim about the community's early theology provisional.

nuance.analogy: Exiguity is like a thin slice of bread that barely covers a plate: there is something there, but very little of it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exiguitas, from exiguus 'small, scanty'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'exiguity' with 'exigency', which means urgent need; the two words have very different meanings.
Using 'exiguity' in casual speech, where 'scarcity' or 'tiny' is more natural.

exiguity.etymology: From Middle French *exiguite*, from Late Latin *exiguitas*.

senses.definition: To free (someone) from an obligation, responsibility or task.
To free (someone) from accusation or blame.

core.definition: To officially clear someone of blame or an accusation, showing that they are not guilty.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on ZAH, and the first syllable is a reduced ih sound. The -rate ending is a flapped r followed by a clear long a.

nuance.connotation: Positive for the person cleared, and a serious word that suggests a formal or public clearing of a reputation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exonerate most often in legal and news contexts, such as when a person is cleared by DNA evidence or by an investigation. In casual talk, people more often say cleared or let off the hook. The word can also mean to free someone from a duty, but that sense is rare in the United States.

distinctions.note: Acquit is a legal term for a court verdict of not guilty. Exonerate is broader and can apply after an investigation or new evidence has shown innocence, even outside a courtroom.
Vindicate means to prove someone was right or justified, often after doubt. Exonerate specifically concerns freedom from blame or guilt.

examples.everyday: After they found the real driver on camera, my neighbor was finally exonerated and his name was cleared.
examples.professional: The internal review fully exonerated the engineering team, so no one was disciplined.
examples.analytical: A theory of justice must explain how the innocent are exonerated, not only how the guilty are punished.

nuance.analogy: To exonerate someone is like taking a stain off a shirt. The accusation is removed, and the person is clean again.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exonerare, to unload or free from a burden, from ex- (out of) and onus (burden).
common_mistakes: Using exonerate as a synonym for excuse in casual speech, when excuse means to forgive a small mistake.
Writing exonerate with the wrong stress, placing it on the last syllable.

exonerate.etymology: From Middle English *exoneraten* (attested in past participle *exonerated*), from Latin *exonerātus*, past perfect participle of *exonerō* (“to discharge, unload; to exonerate”), see *-ate*.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to expiation.

core.definition: Intended to make amends for a sin or wrong, especially through a sacrifice, penance, or ritual act.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EK. The middle syllable a is reduced to uh, and the last syllable is ee. In most American speech the vowel in tawr sounds like the one in caught.

nuance.connotation: Serious and formal. It implies guilt and a deliberate attempt to atone, often in religious or ritual settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expiatory mostly in theological, historical, and literary writing about sacrifice, penance, or ritual. In everyday speech they would say a way of making up for it or an act of atonement. It is rarely needed in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Penitential describes an attitude or practice of repentance; expiatory emphasizes the act of making amends or removing guilt.
Atoning is common and general, while expiatory is more technical and often refers to specific rites or sacrifices.

examples.everyday: Her apology wasn't enough; she wanted some kind of expiatory gesture to show she was really sorry.
examples.professional: The board's expiatory donation was meant to repair public trust after the scandal.
examples.analytical: Ritual expiatory offerings in ancient Israel functioned to cleanse the sanctuary and restore the community's standing before God.

nuance.analogy: An expiatory act is like wiping a stain off a shirt before wearing it again; the mark is removed so the garment is clean.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expiatorius, serving to make atonement, from expiare.
common_mistakes: Using expiatory as a noun; it is only an adjective, so say an expiatory offering, not an expiatory.
Stressing the middle syllable; the main stress falls on EK.

senses.definition: To edit out (incorrect, offensive, or otherwise undesirable information) from a book or other publication; to cleanse; to purge.
senses.example: The publisher decided to expurgate the love scene from the book, to make it more child-friendly.

senses.definition: To undertake editing out incorrect, offensive, or otherwise undesirable information from (a book or other publication); to cleanse; to purge.
senses.example: The publisher decided to expurgate the book, which meant removing the love scene.

core.definition: To remove objectionable or inappropriate material from a text, book, or film before publication or release.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EKS. The middle syllable is a weak, reduced 'per', and the final 'gate' sounds like 'gayt'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It implies that content was cut, often by censors or editors, which may be seen as a loss.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expurgate mostly in literary, historical, and academic discussions of censorship, such as an expurgated edition of a classic novel. In everyday speech, people say 'censor,' 'clean up,' or 'edit out.' The word often appears in phrases like 'expurgated edition' or 'expurgated version.'

distinctions.note: Censor is the general term for suppressing material by authority; expurgate specifically means removing parts of a text, often from an edition.
Edit is the neutral, everyday word for changing a text; expurgate means removing content, usually offensive or inappropriate material.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's copy of that old adventure book is expurgated, so some of the rougher scenes are missing.
examples.professional: The publisher wants to expurgate the training manual before sending it to the international team.
examples.analytical: Victorian editors often expurgated the sexual content of classical texts, which distorted the way readers understood those works.

nuance.analogy: To expurgate a book is like trimming a hedge until it looks tidy, but in doing so you cut away branches that were part of the original plant.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expurgare, 'to purify, cleanse', from ex- 'out' plus purgare 'to cleanse'.
common_mistakes: Using expurgate for simply editing or proofreading; it specifically means removing objectionable material.
Stressing the second syllable, as in eks-PUR-gayt.

expurgate.etymology: From Latin *expurgātus*, perfect passive participle of *expurgō* (“purge, cleanse, purify”).

senses.definition: Something that is extracted or drawn out.
A portion of a book, document, recording etc. incorporated distinctly in another work (for written or spoken words, synonymous to a citation; a quotation).
senses.example: I used an extract of Hemingway's book to demonstrate culture shock.

senses.definition: A decoction, solution, or infusion made by drawing out from any substance that which gives it its essential and characteristic virtue.
senses.example: vanilla extract

senses.definition: Any substance extracted is such a way, and characteristic of that from which it is obtained.
senses.example: quinine is the most important extract of Peruvian bark.

senses.definition: A solid preparation obtained by evaporating a solution of a drug, etc. or the fresh juice of a plant (distinguished from an abstract).
Ancestry; descent.
(Can we verify this sense?) A draft or copy of writing; a certified copy of the proceedings in an action and the judgment therein, with an order for execution.
To draw out; to pull out; to remove forcibly from a fixed position, as by traction or suction, etc.
senses.example: to extract a tooth from its socket, a stump from the earth, or a splinter from the finger

senses.definition: To withdraw by squeezing, distillation, or other mechanical or chemical process. Compare abstract (transitive verb).
senses.example: to extract an essential oil from a plant

senses.definition: To pick out; to cite or reproduce a snippet of.
senses.example: extract a passage from a text.

senses.definition: To select parts of a whole.
senses.example: We need to try to extract the positives from the defeat.

senses.definition: To determine (a root of a number).
senses.example: Please extract the cube root of 27.

core.definition: A concentrated substance drawn from a plant, food, or other source, such as vanilla extract, used for flavor or medicine.

pronunciation.tip: As a noun, stress the first syllable, EK. As a verb, the stress shifts to the second syllable, ik-STRAKT, so the difference is in stress. The flap t is not used here; the t is a light, clear t at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a product or a passage, not a judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use extract most often in cooking and shopping, such as vanilla extract or lemon extract, and in medicine for concentrated plant or herbal products. In academic and professional settings, an extract can be a short passage taken from a book or report. The noun is common, while the verb is more formal.

distinctions.note: Essence is a concentrated liquid used for flavor, often sold in small bottles; extract is more common and can refer to a stronger product or a text passage.
Excerpt is a passage taken from a longer text, while extract can also mean a product or a removed substance.

examples.everyday: Can you grab the vanilla extract from the cabinet? The recipe calls for a teaspoon.
examples.professional: Please include the short extract from the vendor's report in the appendix of our presentation.
examples.analytical: The essay uses a brief extract from Augustine to illustrate the argument about divine grace.

nuance.analogy: Like brewing a strong tea from loose leaves: the essential flavor is drawn out and concentrated.
nuance.etymology: From Latin extrahere, to draw out, from ex- (out) and trahere (to draw).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable in the noun, which makes it sound like the verb.
Using extract when you mean excerpt; extract often suggests a selected passage, but both can be used for written text.

extract.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *extractum*, neuter perfect passive participle of *extrahō*, from *ex-* + *trahō*.

senses.definition: Vision or the faculty of sight.
senses.example: good eyesight

senses.definition: View or the range of vision.

core.definition: The ability of your eyes to see; how clearly you can see with them.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on EYE, and the final syllable has a long i, like the word site. Do not reduce the second part to a weak vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; losing eyesight sounds serious, so the word can carry concern when used about illness or aging.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eyesight in everyday talk about vision, especially for older people or for sports and driving. Phrases like her eyesight is getting worse or I have terrible eyesight sound natural. Vision is the more clinical word, and eyesight feels more personal.

distinctions.note: Vision is more formal and can also mean a future plan; eyesight is everyday and refers to physical seeing.
Sight is the general word and can also mean a view or a famous place; eyesight specifically means the ability to see.

examples.everyday: My grandpa still has pretty good eyesight, so he reads the paper without his glasses.
examples.professional: The safety training requires that all forklift drivers pass an eyesight check before they start.
examples.analytical: Scripture links physical eyesight with spiritual perception, so Isaac's failing eyesight in Genesis becomes a figure for limited understanding.

nuance.analogy: Eyesight is like the lens of a camera: when it is clean and sharp, the picture is clear.
nuance.etymology: Eye (Old English eage) plus sight (Old English gesiht), from the sense of seeing.
common_mistakes: Spelling it eyesite; the correct spelling is eyesight.
Using eyesight for a single view; for a view or a famous place, the word is sight.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word for eye is 'ayin, which often stands for sight and perception. Deuteronomy 34:7 says Moses's eye was not dim when he died, a sign of lasting strength. Genesis 27:1 says Isaac's eyes were dim with age, so he could not reliably see who stood before him. 1 Samuel 3:2 notes that Eli's eyes had begun to grow dim, so he could not see.

senses.definition: Identifying or verifying a person from their face.

core.definition: Technology that identifies or verifies a person by analyzing the features of their face in an image or video.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on NISH in 'recognition,' and 'facial' has a secondary stress on FAY. Americans say 'FAY-shul,' with the vowel reduced, not 'fa-see-al.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical settings, but often debated because of privacy and fairness concerns.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use facial recognition for software that matches faces, for example to unlock a phone or to identify people in images. In news and policy debates it often carries concerns about surveillance and bias. For a phone unlock feature, Americans may say Face ID, which is Apple's brand name.

distinctions.note: Face detection only finds that a face is present, while facial recognition identifies or verifies who the person is.
Biometrics is the broader category of identifying people by physical traits, and facial recognition is one kind of biometric method.

examples.everyday: My phone uses facial recognition to unlock, so I don't have to type a passcode.
examples.professional: Our model's facial recognition accuracy dropped for older users, so we're retraining it with more data.
examples.analytical: Facial recognition raises questions about consent, surveillance, and whether error rates fall unevenly across groups.

nuance.analogy: Facial recognition works like a doorman who matches each face against a guest list, but it does so with numbers instead of memory.
nuance.etymology: Facial comes from Latin facies 'face'; recognition comes from Latin recognoscere 'to know again.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'recognition of facial' instead of 'facial recognition.'
Confusing it with face detection, which finds faces but does not identify them.

conversation.text: Facial recognition matches a face in an image against a database of known faces.
Some facial recognition systems have shown higher error rates for certain demographic groups.
Several cities have debated limits on police use of facial recognition.

senses.definition: In existentialism, the state of being in the world without any knowable reason for such existence, or of being in a particular state of affairs which one has no control over.
The quality or state of being a fact.
A fact that is not changeable or that is assumed to be true without further evaluation.

core.definition: In existentialist philosophy, the given facts of one's situation, such as birth, body, and circumstances, that one did not choose but must live within.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TIS, and the final syllable is a reduced 'tee'. Americans say the middle syllable with a quick, weak vowel, not a full 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical term that describes conditions without judging them.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialized philosophical term, most used in existentialist and phenomenological writing by Sartre, Heidegger, and their interpreters. Outside philosophy, Americans would say 'the facts' or 'the way things are'. In a seminar or academic paper, it is precise and natural; in ordinary talk it would sound overly technical.

distinctions.note: 'Factuality' is the general quality of being factual; 'facticity' in existentialism refers to the unchosen conditions that limit a person's freedom.
Contingency means that something could have been otherwise; facticity means the fixed conditions one actually faces and must take up.

examples.everyday: I know I can't change where I was born, so I just accept that part of my life as a given.
examples.professional: In our ethics seminar, we discussed how a team's facticity, its budget and history, shapes what decisions are actually possible.
examples.analytical: Sartre argues that human freedom operates within facticity, so that our choices are made from a situation we did not select.

nuance.analogy: Facticity is like the table of cards you are dealt in a game: you cannot choose the hand, but you still decide how to play it.
nuance.etymology: Coined in English from 'fact', from Latin factum, 'thing done', with the suffix '-ity'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'factuality' in everyday contexts, where it sounds too technical.
Pronouncing the middle syllable too strongly, as 'fak-TIH-sih-tee'.

facticity.etymology: From *fact* + *icity*, possibly modelled on German *Faktizität* which first appeared in the writings of the German philosopher Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762–1814).

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or caused by factions.
Given to or characterized by discordance or insubordination.

core.definition: Causing or characterized by division, conflict, or rebellion within a group, especially by stirring up disagreement.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, FAK, and the ending is a quick 'shus'. Keep the 'ch' sound out of it, since it is 'sh' as in 'ocean'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes people who deliberately create division or resist authority.
nuance.usage_note: This word appears mainly in formal writing, political commentary, and history. Americans would more often say 'divisive' or 'disruptive' in everyday speech. Calling a colleague 'factious' in a meeting would sound harsh and old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: 'Divisive' is common and describes something that splits people apart; 'factious' implies deliberate stirring up of rival groups.
'Disruptive' is general and everyday; 'factious' is more specific to political or group conflict.

examples.everyday: Stop being so factious at dinner; we are all on the same side.
examples.professional: The manager asked the team to stop the factious arguments and focus on the shared launch goal.
examples.analytical: Hobbes saw the factious spirit of groups within the commonwealth as a threat to peace and sovereignty.

nuance.analogy: A factious group is like a family that keeps picking fights to split the household into camps.
nuance.etymology: From Latin factiosus, 'of a faction', from factio, 'party or group'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'fictitious', which means made up or false.
Using it for simple disagreement; it implies deliberate division.

factious.etymology: From Latin *factiosus* (“divisive; inclined to separate”); derivative of *factio*.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to feudalism.

core.definition: Relating to feudalism, the medieval system in which land was granted to lords in exchange for loyalty and military service.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the second syllable as a weak 'dul,' not 'dahl.' The first vowel sounds like the word 'few.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in historical discussion. In modern commentary, it is often negative, as in 'feudal management' meaning rigid, inherited power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use 'feudal' in history classes, political analysis, and writing about medieval society. Outside those settings, it is often used metaphorically for an unfair, rigid system, and this can sound pointed or critical. Say 'a feudal system' or 'feudal lords' when describing history.

distinctions.note: 'Medieval' names a whole historical era, while 'feudal' names one specific social and legal system within it.
'Manorial' refers to the manor, the local estate; 'feudal' covers the wider system of land and obligations among lords and vassals.
'Autocratic' describes absolute personal rule, whereas 'feudal' describes a decentralized hierarchy of obligations.

examples.everyday: My history teacher said the feudal system ended slowly, not all at once.
examples.professional: Our internal approval process is so feudal that every team lead controls their own budget with no oversight.
examples.analytical: Marc Bloch argued that feudal society was defined less by a single institution than by a web of personal dependence and mutual obligation.

nuance.analogy: A feudal system is like a pyramid of favors: each person owes service upward and receives protection downward.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin feudalis, from feudum, meaning fief or land held in exchange for service.
common_mistakes: Using 'feudal' as a noun; the noun is 'feudalism.'
Saying 'FOO-dal' with the vowel of 'food' in the first syllable; it sounds like 'few.'

feudal.etymology: From Old French *feodal*, from Medieval Latin *feodalis*, from *feodum*, *feudum*, *fevum* (“fief, fee”), from **fehu* (“cattle, owndom, property, fee”), from Proto-Germanic **fehu* (“cattle”).

senses.definition: Of or relating to fire.
Burning or glowing.
Inflammable or easily ignited.
Having the color of fire.
Hot or inflamed.
Tempestuous or emotionally volatile; sulfurous.
senses.example: a fiery temper

senses.definition: Spirited or filled with emotion.
Having the capillaries contracted due to stress at time of slaughter, causing blood to not drain properly.

core.definition: Literally burning or glowing like fire; figuratively, passionate, angry or full of energy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is quick, and the final -y is a light 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Mostly positive when praising passion, energy or spirit; negative when describing anger or a hot temper.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fiery for a spicy food, a red sunset, a passionate speech or a temper. It is common in everyday talk: 'That chili is fiery' is natural. Describing a person as fiery usually suggests strong emotion and is generally polite.

distinctions.note: Passionate describes deep feeling in general, while fiery adds a sense of visible heat, energy or temper.
Spicy describes food flavor; fiery can describe food, but also emotion, color or speech.

examples.everyday: That salsa is so fiery that I needed a glass of milk right away.
examples.professional: She gave a fiery presentation that convinced the leadership team to fund the project.
examples.analytical: The prophet's fiery language draws on imagery of burning altars and purifying flame.

nuance.analogy: A fiery speech is like a campfire that spreads its heat across the whole room.
nuance.etymology: From fire, from Old English fyr, meaning fire.
common_mistakes: Saying 'FY-ree' with the wrong vowel; the middle syllable is 'ur' as in 'fire'.
Using fiery for a cold or calm person, which sounds contradictory.
nuance.biblical_note: Fiery in Scripture often describes God's presence, judgment or the spiritual battle, using the Hebrew word saraph, meaning to burn. Numbers 21:6 describes fiery serpents sent among the Israelites in the wilderness. Deuteronomy 8:15 recalls the same wilderness and its fiery serpents, while Ephesians 6:16 speaks of the flaming darts of the evil one that faith can quench.

fiery.etymology: From Middle English *fyry*, from *fyr* (“fire”), equivalent to *fire* + *-y*.

senses.definition: A tactic (such as giving long, often irrelevant speeches) employed to delay the proceedings of, or the making of a decision by, a legislative body, particularly the United States Senate.
A member of a legislative body causing such an obstruction.

(historical) A mercenary soldier; a freebooter; specifically, a mercenary who traveled illegally in an organized group from the United States to a country in Central America or the Spanish West Indies in the mid-19th century seeking economic and political benefits through armed force.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To take part in a private military action in a foreign country.
To use obstructionist tactics in a legislative body.

core.definition: A tactic in a legislative body, especially the U.S. Senate, in which a member prolongs debate to block a vote.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The last syllable is 'ster', with the r pronounced and the vowel reduced, not 'boo-ster'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral, depending on the speaker's politics; supporters call it a defense of minority rights and critics call it obstruction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use filibuster mainly in news and political talk about the Senate, where the 60-vote threshold for cloture ends most filibusters. Saying 'they are filibustering' is common during heated debates. The word is not used for ordinary meetings, though people may jokingly say someone is filibustering a conversation.

distinctions.note: Debate is a normal exchange of arguments; a filibuster is a deliberate strategy to delay a decision.
Obstruction is a broader term for blocking progress; a filibuster is a specific parliamentary tactic.

examples.everyday: The Senate has been stuck on that bill because of a filibuster.
examples.professional: Our project review got bogged down by a filibuster of comments that kept repeating the same objection.
examples.analytical: The filibuster illustrates how procedural rules can shape substantive policy outcomes.

nuance.analogy: Like someone holding the microphone for hours so the meeting cannot end.
nuance.etymology: From Dutch vrijbuiter (freebooter), via Spanish and French, originally meaning a pirate or mercenary.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as 'boo-ster'.
Using it as a verb about any long meeting without the legislative sense.

filibuster.etymology: Spanish *filibustero* (“pirate”), from French *flibustier*, ultimately from Dutch *vrijbuiter* (“freebooter”), from *vrij* (“free”) + *buit* (“booty”) + *-er* (“agent”).

core.definition: Describing the earliest ripened fruit of a season, such as figs or grapes, which the Bible treats as especially prized and dedicated to God.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FIRST in this hyphenated compound, with ripe lighter. Pronounce the vowel in ripe as a long i diphthong, like 'ryp', not 'reep'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests early blessing and promise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use this word outside Bible study, sermons and religious writing. In ordinary talk people say 'the first ripe figs' or 'early figs.' Use it when you are discussing the Bible or the agriculture of ancient Israel.

distinctions.note: Firstfruits is the offering or the harvest itself; first-ripe describes a fruit or crop as the earliest to ripen.
Early is a general word for before the usual time; first-ripe is specific to the first fruit of a season in biblical language.

examples.everyday: Grandma's fig tree gave us the first-ripe figs of the summer, and she made us save a few for the church picnic.
examples.professional: The preacher explained the first-ripe offering in Numbers, and some of the youth group had never heard the term before.
examples.analytical: The prophet's image of first-ripe figs presents Israel as a rare and desired fruit that the Lord notices early, before the rest of the harvest.

nuance.analogy: Like the first peach from a backyard tree in June, which tastes better than the ones that follow.
nuance.etymology: From Old English fyrst, 'first', and ripe, from Old English ripe, 'ready to be harvested'.
common_mistakes: Using first-ripe as a noun, when it is normally an adjective before a noun
Stressing ripe instead of first in the compound
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word bikkurah (bikkurah), meaning first-ripe fruit, appears in the Old Testament for the first produce of a harvest that belonged to the Lord. Numbers 13:20 describes the season of the first-ripe grapes when the spies entered the land. Isaiah 28:4 compares a people's early fate to a first-ripe fig that is eaten as soon as it is seen. Hosea 9:10 recalls God's delight in Israel as the first-ripe fruit on the fig tree, and then describes how Israel turned away to shameful idols.

senses.definition: Showing disrespect through a casual attitude, levity, and a lack of due seriousness; pert.
Loquacious; speaking with ease and rapidity.
Nimble; limber.

core.definition: Showing a careless, disrespectful attitude, especially when a serious matter deserves respect.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FLIP. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, so say it as a quick un, and do not add an extra vowel before the final t.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a tone or remark that seems careless or rude about something important.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use flippant to criticize casual remarks made at the wrong time, such as a joke at a funeral or a dismissive answer to a serious question. It is stronger than casual and suggests disrespect. People often say that is flippant or don't be flippant when they want someone to be serious.

distinctions.note: Playful is friendly and light, while flippant suggests a careless or disrespectful dismissal of something that matters.
Casual describes an relaxed manner, while flippant adds the sense of disrespect toward serious matters.

examples.everyday: Don't be flippant when I tell you the doctor called, because it's serious.
examples.professional: His flippant reply to the security concern made the review meeting tense.
examples.analytical: The philosopher calls such flippant dismissals of conscience a failure of moral seriousness.

nuance.analogy: A flippant remark is like skipping a step on a staircase: it looks quick, but it misses what matters.
nuance.etymology: From an earlier sense meaning nimble or talkative, from Latin roots for light or quick.
common_mistakes: Using flippant to mean fun or cheerful without any disrespect.
Confusing flippant with frivolous, which means silly or unimportant rather than disrespectful.

flippant.etymology: 1595, from Northern English dialectal *flippand* (“prattling, babbling, glib”), present participle of *flip* (“to babble”), of origin.

senses.definition: A sport played on foot in which teams attempt to get a ball into a goal or zone defended by the other team.
senses.example: Roman and medieval football matches were more violent than any modern type of football.

senses.definition: The ball used in any game called "football".
senses.example: The player kicked the football.

senses.definition: American football: a game played on a field 100 yards long and 53 1/3 yards wide in which two teams of 11 players attempt to get an ovoid ball to the end of each other's territory.
senses.example: Each team scored two touchdowns when they played football.

senses.definition: Canadian football: a game played on a field 110 yards long and 65 yards wide in which two teams of 12 players attempt to get an ovoid ball to the end of each other's territory.
senses.example: They played football in the snow.

senses.definition: Any form of rugby. rugby league.
Practice of these particular games, or techniques used in them.
An item of discussion, particularly in a back-and-forth manner.
senses.example: That budget item became a political football.

senses.definition: The leather briefcase containing classified nuclear war plans which is always near the US President.
(rare) To play football.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: In the United States, a sport played by two teams of eleven players on a field, using an oval ball and a goal line.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FUT. The second syllable is a light 'ball' with a vowel close to 'aw', so say 'FUT-bawl'. Do not stress both syllables equally.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a common sport name that is often associated with American culture, especially on weekends and holidays.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'football' means American football unless the context says otherwise. For the sport most of the world calls football, Americans say 'soccer'. If you say 'football' to mean soccer, people will think you mean the NFL. You can say 'Are you watching football this weekend?' in casual talk, and 'the big football game' often refers to a college or NFL contest.

distinctions.note: 'Soccer' is the American word for the sport played with feet and no hand contact; 'football' in the US means American football.
'Rugby' is a different sport with an oval ball and no forward passing; Americans sometimes mistake it for football.

examples.everyday: Do you want to come over and watch football on Sunday?
examples.professional: Our marketing team is sponsoring the college football bowl game this December.
examples.analytical: Sociologists have argued that American football functions as a civic ritual that brings together regional and class identities.

nuance.analogy: Football is like a chess match on a field: every play is a planned move, and the teams are constantly testing each other's strategy.
nuance.etymology: From 'foot' and 'ball', originally referring to games played on foot rather than on horseback.
common_mistakes: Using 'football' to mean soccer when speaking to Americans, which causes confusion.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'foot-BALL'.

conversation.text: Are you watching football this Sunday?
We usually have people over to watch college football on Saturdays.
My son wants to play football, but I'm worried about injuries.

senses.definition: A low stool for supporting the feet while seated.
Anything trodden upon or treated as subservient.

core.definition: A low stool or padded support on which a seated person rests their feet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FUT. The second syllable rhymes with 'pool', so say 'stool' with a long 'oo' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and comfortable. It describes a household object.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'footstool' for a small padded seat or ottoman placed in front of a chair or sofa. In modern American homes, many people say 'ottoman' for the same object, especially if it is upholstered and can hold a tray. A natural request is 'Can you put your feet up on the footstool?'

distinctions.note: An ottoman is often larger and upholstered, and may also serve as extra seating; a footstool is usually smaller and simpler.
A stool is a seat without a back; a footstool is for resting the feet, not for sitting on normally.

collocations: put your feet on a footstool

examples.everyday: Grandma always keeps a little footstool next to her armchair.
examples.professional: For the ergonomic review, we added a footstool to the standing desk setup.
examples.analytical: Psalm 110 describes God's enemies as a footstool, a picture of complete and humbling subjection.

nuance.analogy: A footstool is like a small landing for your feet: it lifts them slightly so you can relax fully.
nuance.etymology: From 'foot' and 'stool', literally a stool for the feet.
common_mistakes: Using 'footstool' for a bench or chair with a back; it is only for resting feet.
Confusing 'footstool' with 'footrest', which is usually a fixed bar or attachment.
nuance.biblical_note: Footstool is a symbol of authority and subjection in Scripture. Psalm 110:1 has the Lord say to the king, sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool. Isaiah 66:1 says heaven is God's throne and the earth his footstool, and Matthew 5:35 echoes this image. The Hebrew word hadom means footstool, a symbol of royal dominion.

senses.definition: A penalty for or consequence of a misdemeanor.
A thing forfeited; that which is taken from somebody in requital of a misdeed committed; that which is lost, or the right to which is alienated, by a crime, breach of contract, etc.
senses.example: He who murders pays the forfeit of his own life.

senses.definition: Something deposited and redeemable by a sportive fine as part of a game.
Injury; wrong; mischief.
To suffer the loss of something by wrongdoing or non-compliance.
senses.example: He forfeited his last chance of an early release from jail by repeatedly attacking another inmate.

senses.definition: To lose a contest, game, match, or other form of competition by voluntary withdrawal, by failing to attend or participate, or by violation of the rules.
senses.example: Because only nine players were present, the football team was forced to forfeit the game.

senses.definition: To be guilty of a misdeed; to be criminal; to transgress.
To fail to keep an obligation.
Of government officials: to legally remove property from its previous owners.
